chunks: My father (rah) said: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father from Ali ibn Ma'bad from Wasil ibn Abdullah from Abdullah ibn Sinan from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said one day to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him): 'Shall I give you good tidings?' He said: 'Yes, my father and mother be sacrificed for you, for you have always been giving good tidings of every good.'
He said: 'Gabriel informed me just now of the amazing thing.'
The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'And what did he inform you of, O Messenger of Allah?'

He said: 'He informed me that when a man from my ummah sends blessings upon me and follows it by sending blessings upon my Ahl al-Bayt, the gates of heaven are opened for him, and the angels send seventy blessings upon him, and it is an expiation for sins.'
Then the sins fall away from him as leaves fall from the tree.
And Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, says: 'Answer him, O My angels; you send blessings upon him seventy times, and I send seven hundred blessings upon him.'
So if he sends blessings upon me but does not follow it by sending blessings upon my Ahl al-Bayt, there are seventy veils between that [blessing] and the heaven.
And Allah, Glorious is His Majesty, says: 'There is no answer for him and no fortune for him, O My angels; do not raise his supplication unless he joins the progeny to the Prophet.'
So he remains veiled until he joins my Ahl al-Bayt [to his blessings upon me].
ai.seo_question: What is the reward of sending blessings upon the Prophet and his progeny together?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-A’mal* underscores the Shia theological emphasis on the inseparability of the Prophet’s authority from his Ahl al-Bayt, framing salawat as a means of spiritual elevation and sin expiation. The mention of seventy angelic prayers and divine response highlights the metaphysical weight of this practice, while the 'seventy veils' for neglecting the progeny illustrate the conditional nature of accepted supplication in Shia tradition.
